analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal tax deduction for prescription drug ads aimed at consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 22 Senate cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the Finance Committee before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug companies can currently write off the cost of television, magazine, and internet ads aimed at consumers, so federal taxpayers effectively subsidize part of the roughly $6 billion a year spent on prescription drug marketing [S2][S3]. The bill would remove that deduction, raising federal revenue and slightly raising the cost to drugmakers of marketing directly to patients. It was introduced in January 2021, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and patients, in a modest way. The bill would raise federal revenue by denying drugmakers a business deduction, and by making consumer drug advertising more expensive it could reduce the ad-driven push of expensive brand-name drugs that nudges patients and insurers toward higher-cost prescriptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and patients paying drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any federal income tax deduction for expenses of direct-to-consumer advertising of prescription drugs, including TV, radio, print, direct mail, billboards, and internet or social media ads.
Applies to amounts paid or incurred after enactment, ending a subsidy under which taxpayers effectively absorb part of the cost of drug marketing.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies, which would pay higher taxes on marketing spending, and the media and advertising industries, which would lose some of the billions in revenue that prescription drug ads generate.

drawbacks.text: Tax deductibility of ordinary business expenses is a long-standing norm; singling out one industry's advertising breaks that pattern and invites the same treatment for other products lawmakers dislike.

The tax cost falls on drugmakers, not the ads themselves: firms could shift marketing budgets toward physicians and other channels, and direct-to-consumer ads can also inform patients about treatments they did not know existed.
Media outlets, already strained by ad revenue losses, would lose part of a category of advertising they rely on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, targeted change: it ends a specific tax break rather than banning the ads, and the revenue and reduced pressure toward heavily advertised brand-name drugs are real but not transformative. The main honest costs are the break with neutral tax treatment and the risk that marketing dollars simply move to channels the bill does not touch.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2021, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 117th Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on January 28, 2021, with 21 original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
It attracted 22 cosponsors in total, all Democrats or independents, but no further action was ever taken and the Congress ended without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies keep the federal tax deduction for consumer drug advertising, and media companies keep the ad revenue; taxpayers continue to absorb part of the cost through the tax code.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and their ad sellers

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny the tax deduction for direct-to-consumer prescription drug ads.

for.name: 22 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 20 of 48 Senate Democrats and 2 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican cosponsored the bill, and it never reached a vote.

industries.note: Drugmakers would lose the tax write-off for the ads they aim at consumers, which push patients toward high-priced brand-name drugs; that cost is currently shared with taxpayers and drives demand that supports higher drug prices.

industries.industry: Broadcast, publishing, and digital advertising/media companies
industries.note: Prescription drug ads are a major ad category across TV and digital platforms; removing the deduction would shrink that revenue stream.
